title: Hidden Magnetic Octupolar Order driven by Spin-Orbit coupling in KFeF$_3$
authors: C. A. Crawford, C. I. Hiley, N. C. Bristowe, C. Stock, J. Gainza, C. Ritter, M. R. Lees, R. I. Walton, M. S. Senn
abstract: Phase transitions are typically driven by symmetry-breaking structural distortions that lift electronic degeneracies, yet in some cases, these transitions may be driven by a hidden order without conventional structural signatures. Here, we demonstrate that the 3$d$ perovskite, KFeF$_3$, hosts such a hidden instability. Using a combination of high-resolution powder diffraction, magnetometry, symmetry-based analysis and first principles calculations, we reveal that while the 90 K cubic to rhombohedral transition arises from conventional magnetostriction accompanying antiferromagnetic order, a second transition at 40 K lowers the symmetry to monoclinic without any detectable Jahn-Teller distortion or translational symmetry-breaking. Symmetry-based Landau analysis supports a hidden zone centered magnetic octupole order parameter, whose improper coupling accounts for the weak ferromagnetism and pronounced symmetry-breaking strain. Density functional calculations show that spin-orbit coupling suppresses the competing Jahn-Teller instability, and thereby favors higher rank magnetic multipolar degrees of freedom. These findings establish KFeF$_3$ as a model system in which the competing energy scales between spin-orbit coupling and orbital degeneracy result in the emergence of hidden, multipolar order. We show that the control of such magnetic, multipolar order could, in principle, provide a route to induce altermagnetism.
summary: This work demonstrates that the material KFeF3 undergoes a low-temperature phase transition driven by a hidden magnetic octupole order, rather than conventional structural distortion. The key mechanism involves spin-orbit coupling stabilizing this higher-rank magnetic order, which is responsible for observed weak ferromagnetism. The study establishes KFeF3 as a model system for understanding multipolar magnetism driven by competing electronic energy scales.
main_problem: The study investigates phase transitions driven by 'hidden order'—magnetic or structural instabilities lacking conventional symmetry-breaking signatures.
main_result: The low-temperature transition in KFeF3 is driven by a hidden magnetic octupole order parameter, which is stabilized by spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and accounts for weak ferromagnetism.
method: The research combines high-resolution powder diffraction, magnetometry, symmetry-based Landau analysis, and first-principles DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is the 3d perovskite, KFeF3, which exhibits multiple magnetic and structural transitions between cubic, rhombohedral, and monoclinic phases.
key_observables: Weak ferromagnetism (wFM), symmetry-breaking strain, magnetic octupole order parameter, and the evolution of the effective magnetic moment ($\mu_{	ext{eff}}$).
important_parameters: The competition between spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and orbital degeneracy, which dictates the emergence of higher-rank magnetic multipolar degrees of freedom.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on symmetry-based Landau theory and DFT calculations to model the coupling between different magnetic multipolar orders.
figures_summary: Figures show magnetic susceptibility (M(T), M(H)), variable temperature neutron diffraction data confirming structural transitions, and theoretical diagrams illustrating the coupling of the octupole order parameter to strain and weak ferromagnetism.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from characterizing conventional transitions (90 K) to identifying the hidden instability (40 K). It uses symmetry analysis (Landau theory) to pinpoint the octupole order, and DFT calculations confirm the role of SOC in suppressing competing instabilities and stabilizing the multipolar state.
why_interesting: The concept of hidden, multipolar order driven by SOC is highly relevant to understanding exotic magnetic states in strongly correlated materials, which often exhibit complex, non-collinear magnetic ground states.
